Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{1}{y}$ that lies between $y=1$ and $y=2,$ as shown above. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{y})=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y})\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}\sqrt{{y}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3b9798a1-1cad-5e9e-af70-d906e8caaafa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 9-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+4{x}^{2}.$ Then, $x\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}(\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{[\frac{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}{3}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\sqrt{{9}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x\sqrt{1 + \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2 = 4.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176209 :question/id #uuid "4c05778a-860e-50f5-bcb4-539729cfbaeb" :question/math-academy-id "q-104529"} {:db/id 17592186176238 :question/id #uuid Functions of X"}] :question/problem "Consider the arc of the curve $y=x^3-3x$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?

![](images/77/777c36689da6f6cbcf4ce92a7c5ba17c000a7c442a972851d9d1cafaa9fb2ba4.png)" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-3x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-3) & =0 \\ x & =0,\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x= \sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-3x)=3{x}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}x\sqrt{1+(3{x}^{2}-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}x\sqrt{9{x}^{4}-18{x}^{2}+10}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

:tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis. We can also obtain surfaces of revolution by rotating a curve $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.

Consider the arc of the curve $x=f(y)$ that lies between the horizontal lines $y=y_1$ and $y=y_2.$ By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis, we get a surface of revolution, as shown below on the right. How can we calculate its surface area?

![](images/e6/e61f97b06c3228bb2671429d6562e97d6cdefefb7ac1acca31867eeb440a75ff.png)

First, we divide the interval $[y_1,y_2]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{y}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $y$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](images/25/253837a6c151a74318b2e172e6db068a50d23c9cb93124588ae20a9379d9aa63.png)

If $\Delta{y}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $x=f(y).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=x=f(y).$ 

![](images/9f/9f10812beff0283e6029145b854a2faaa9b7a566751bd17514bc6817ef664dfc.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi x \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s
$$
